Shivamogga: Four months of heavy monsoon and cold weather that bring thick fog have transformed the Agumbe Ghat, along National Highway 169A that connects Thirthahalli to Malpe in Udupi, into a high-risk journey for commuters. The scenic ghat roads are a nightmare for commuters due to missing safety barriers, fading road markings and the constant threat of landslides.As vehicles enter Shivamogga district after passing Someshwar in Udupi, the roads are very narrow and fog sets in suddenly, dropping visibility very low. Drivers mostly rely on parking lights to drive. The descent from Agumbe toward the plains is particularly dangerous for light vehicles like cars and motorbikes, as any minor steering error or brake failure at turns lacking protective barriers can send vehicles plunging into gorges.Navigational aids such as white and yellow boundary lines have completely worn off across major stretches. The plastic radium road studs along the roads fail to reflect light properly, and a crucial 2-kilometre stretch at the top of the ghat lacks studs entirely.During the monsoon, strong winds frequently uproot trees onto the highway, leaving travellers waiting for hours for blockages to be cleared.Heavy machinery used for road levelling during summer leaves behind vibrations that loosen rocks.
...

Deep cracks appeared along the road shoulders due to clogged drains and 15-20-tonne trucks operating during the dry season.Regarding these concerns, Lokesh G, executive engineer for National Highways, said a Rs 14 crore development proposal has been submitted to improve the route along the jungle cutting and crash barrier installations where it is viable.However, PWD engineer HS Shashidhar clarified that while metal crash barriers are installed where they are necessary, placing a barrier at the vulnerable sixth hairpin curve is currently not feasible because buses would lack the required turning radius to negotiate the bend safely without road widening. “This structural limitation creates a terrifying experience for bus passengers sitting in front, as the front overhang of large buses hangs 3 to 4 feet out over the valley floor while manoeuvring tight bends,” he said. Due to this issue, locals, bus drivers and community leaders are seeking a solution.PWD minister Satish Jarkiholi recently inspected the site from both Shivamogga and Udupi sides. He said the department is coordinating with the forest department to get necessary approvals for a comprehensive road-widening project while also hinting at a tunnel proposal. However, the proposal has sparked debate among stakeholders. Environmental activists have questioned the ecological feasibility of a mega-tunnel project in the wake of disastrous landslides in Wayanad.Meanwhile, experts said standard road widening would require complete closure of the crucial route for at least two years.

   https://www.daijiworld.com/news/newsDisplay?newsID=1292613
   Kundapur, Sept 17: Agumbe Ghat — one of Karnataka’s most scenic yet treacherous hill routes — has become a nightmare for commuters, with massive potholes dotting almost every hairpin bend.
...
The deteriorating road condition has led to frequent traffic snarls and heightened accident risks, despite a ban on heavy vehicles following recent monsoon-triggered landslips.
...
The ghat stretch, part of the Malpe-Thirthahalli National Highway 169A, includes 14 sharp hairpin bends. A minor landslip at the 12th bend has dumped soil and foliage onto the roadside, while collapsed sidewalls at several turns have raised serious safety concerns.
...
Drainage lines along the ghat are choked with silt, worsening water stagnation and accelerating road damage. Potholes, deep and wide, have appeared at nearly every curve, turning uphill and downhill driving into a dangerous ordeal. Commuters say even a moment's distraction could prove fatal.
...
The poor state of the road is causing routine traffic jams as vehicles slow down or struggle to navigate the uneven bends. “Sometimes we get stuck for up to half an hour, especially if a car stalls while climbing. These potholes are getting worse every day,” said Sunil, a local driver who plies the ghat daily.
...
With the monsoon waning, the region is witnessing a sharp increase in tourist footfall. But the very charm of the ghat — its lush beauty and cool climate — is now overshadowed by its dangerous stretches. Tourists unfamiliar with the terrain are particularly vulnerable, locals warn.
...
Authorities had earlier restricted heavy vehicles from using the route due to minor landslips, but the road remains open to light vehicles — cars, mini-buses, and two-wheelers — all of which are now at risk. “It’s not just a matter of inconvenience anymore. These potholes are accident traps,” Shetty added, urging the concerned departments to act swiftly.
...
The 21-kilometre stretch between Agumbe and Hebri is especially narrow, with blind curves that demand precision driving. Locals believe that only a full-fledged road widening project and proper ghat-edge reinforcement can ensure safety. “Until that happens, we’re at the mercy of weather and luck,” Sunil remarked.
...
Agumbe Ghat, once hailed as the gateway to the Western Ghats’ beauty, is now better known for its perilous drive. With increasing tourist traffic and recurring landslips, urgent intervention is needed. Locals and commuters alike are demanding immediate repairs before the road claims more lives.
